title: Net Present Value & Internal Rate of Return (CMA P2-E · feeds BAR)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — does the excavator clear the hurdle?

With the cash flows estimated, MBG evaluates the investment with discounted-cash-flow methods. Net present value (NPV) and internal rate of return (IRR) are the two that account for the time value of money, and they are the heart of CMA Part 2's investment topic. We use a single illustrative equipment project throughout: initial outlay $400,000, after-tax operating cash flow $120,000 per year for 5 years, discounted at MBG's 10% required rate (close to the WACC from month 8).

Net present value

NPV discounts every future cash flow to today and subtracts the initial outlay:

NPV = present value of inflows − initial investment.

The present-value annuity factor for 5 years at 10% is 3.7908. Present value of inflows = $120,000 × 3.7908 = $454,896. NPV = $454,896 − $400,000 = $54,896. The decision rule: accept if NPV > 0. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the 10% required return and adds $54,896 of value today. NPV is expressed in dollars and is additive across projects.

Internal rate of return

IRR is the discount rate that makes NPV exactly zero — the project's own compound return. For this project, the rate that equates $120,000 × (annuity factor) to $400,000 is about 15.2% (the 5-year factor of $400,000 ÷ $120,000 = 3.3333 falls between the 15% and 16% factors). The decision rule: accept if IRR > the required rate (WACC). Here 15.2% > 10%, so accept — consistent with the positive NPV. For a single conventional project, NPV and IRR always agree on accept/reject.

When NPV and IRR disagree

For mutually exclusive projects (you can pick only one) or projects of different size or timing, NPV and IRR can rank differently. The cause is the reinvestment assumption: NPV implicitly reinvests interim cash flows at the WACC (realistic), while IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself (often unrealistically high). NPV is preferred when they conflict because it measures the actual dollar value created. IRR can also produce multiple or no solutions when cash flows change sign more than once (non-conventional). The modified IRR (MIRR) addresses the reinvestment flaw by reinvesting at the WACC.

Reading the result

A $54,896 NPV is not just "profitable" — it is the value, in today's dollars, created over and above the 10% cost of capital. If two excavators were mutually exclusive, MBG would choose the one with the higher NPV, not the higher IRR. And a project with a positive NPV but a long payback (next week) may still strain liquidity and bonding even though it creates value — which is why payback and the profitability index complement NPV.

Uneven cash flows and the NPV profile

The annuity shortcut works only when cash flows are level; real projects are lumpy, so each year is discounted separately. For cash flows of $150,000, $200,000, and $250,000 in years one through three at 10%, the present values are $150,000 ÷ 1.10 = $136,364, $200,000 ÷ 1.21 = $165,289, and $250,000 ÷ 1.331 = $187,829, summing to $489,482; against a $400,000 outlay, NPV = $89,482. Discounting year by year is the general method the annuity factor only abbreviates.

Plotting a project's NPV against a range of discount rates traces its NPV profile, a downward-sloping curve that crosses zero at the IRR. When two mutually exclusive projects' profiles are drawn together, they intersect at the crossover rate — the discount rate at which they have equal NPV. Below the crossover rate one project leads; above it, the other. This is precisely why NPV and IRR can disagree on mutually exclusive projects: IRR picks the higher internal return, but if the firm's cost of capital sits below the crossover rate, the project with the lower IRR may have the higher NPV and create more value.

MIRR and resolving the conflict

The modified internal rate of return (MIRR) fixes IRR's unrealistic reinvestment assumption. It compounds all interim cash inflows forward to the final year at the cost of capital (not the IRR) to get a terminal value, then finds the single rate that equates the present value of the outflows to that terminal value. Because MIRR reinvests at the realistic WACC, it gives a more reliable percentage measure and resolves much of the NPV-versus-IRR conflict, though for a strict accept/reject or ranking decision NPV remains the standard.

The hierarchy to remember: for a single conventional project, NPV and IRR agree. For mutually exclusive projects that differ in scale or timing, trust NPV because it measures dollar value created and reinvests at the cost of capital. Under capital rationing, where good projects compete for a limited budget, rank by the profitability index (next week) to maximize value per scarce dollar. And whenever cash flows change sign more than once, distrust IRR — it may have multiple values or none — and use NPV or MIRR.

Why the discount rate dominates

NPV is acutely sensitive to the discount rate, which is why month eight's WACC discipline matters here. A long-dated project discounted one point too low looks far more attractive than it is, because the error compounds across every future year. Capital-budgeting practice therefore pairs the NPV with a sensitivity analysis on the discount rate and the key cash-flow drivers, so the decision rests on a range of outcomes rather than a single point estimate that hides how fragile the result is to its assumptions.

One more reconciliation point

It helps to hold the relationships straight. When a project's IRR exceeds the cost of capital, its NPV is positive — the two rules agree to accept. When the IRR equals the cost of capital, NPV is exactly zero. And when the IRR is below the cost of capital, NPV is negative — both reject. The disagreement only appears in ranking mutually exclusive projects, never in a simple accept/reject on a single conventional project. Keeping that map in mind prevents the classic exam error of rejecting a value-creating project because a competing one shows a flashier internal rate of return; the firm-value-maximizing choice is always the higher NPV at the firm's actual cost of capital, with IRR and MIRR serving as the intuitive percentage companions to that dollar decision. In short: NPV decides, IRR and MIRR explain, and on a mutually exclusive choice the project that adds the most dollars of value beats the one with the prettier percentage every time.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR tests NPV computation from an annuity factor, the accept-if-positive rule, the definition of IRR, and the reinvestment-assumption reason NPV is preferred for mutually exclusive projects. Expect a question where the higher-IRR project has the lower NPV and you must choose by NPV.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute NPV as present value of inflows minus the initial outlay; accept if positive.
  2. Understand IRR as the rate that zeroes NPV; accept if it exceeds the WACC.
  3. Prefer NPV for mutually exclusive projects because of the reinvestment assumption.
  4. Watch for multiple/no IRR with non-conventional cash flows; consider MIRR.

Recap: the project's NPV is $54,896 at a 10% rate and its IRR is about 15.2%, so both methods say accept. When methods conflict on mutually exclusive projects, NPV wins because it reinvests at the realistic cost of capital and measures dollar value created.

quiz.title: Net Present Value and Internal Rate of Return

questions.q: Inflows are $120,000/year for 5 years (annuity factor 3.7908 at 10%); the outlay is $400,000. NPV is:
The NPV decision rule is to accept a project when NPV is:
questions.explain: A positive NPV means the project earns more than the required return and adds value.

questions.q: The internal rate of return is the discount rate at which:
questions.explain: IRR is the rate that makes net present value exactly zero.

questions.q: A project's IRR is 15.2% and the required rate (WACC) is 10%. Under the IRR rule, MBG should:
choices: Accept it because IRR exceeds the WACC
questions.explain: Accept when IRR exceeds the required rate; 15.2% > 10%.

questions.q: For mutually exclusive projects where NPV and IRR rank differently, which method is preferred and why?
choices: IRR, because it is a percentage
NPV, because it reinvests at the WACC and measures dollar value
questions.explain: NPV uses the realistic WACC reinvestment assumption and measures actual value created.

questions.q: Non-conventional cash flows (sign changes more than once) can cause IRR to:
questions.explain: Multiple sign changes can yield multiple IRRs or none; MIRR or NPV is more reliable.

questions.q: A $54,896 positive NPV at a 10% rate means the project:
choices: Creates $54,896 of value today above the 10% cost of capital
questions.explain: Positive NPV is value created in today's dollars beyond the required return.
